passages.text: Modulation of epileptic activity by deep brain stimulation: a model-based study of frequency-dependent effects

A number of studies showed that deep brain stimulation (DBS) can modulate the activity in the epileptic brain and that a decrease of seizures can be achieved in “responding” patients. <sentence_start/>In most of these studies, the choice of stimulation parameters is critical to obtain desired clinical effects. <sentence_start/>In particular, the stimulation frequency is a key parameter that is difficult to tune. <sentence_start/>A reason is that our knowledge about the frequency-dependant mechanisms according to which DBS indirectly impacts the dynamics of pathological neuronal systems located in the neocortex is still limited. <sentence_start/>We address this issue using both computational modeling and intracerebral EEG (iEEG) data. <sentence_start/>We developed a macroscopic (neural mass) model of the thalamocortical network. <sentence_start/>In line with already-existing models, it includes interconnected neocortical pyramidal cells and interneurons, thalamocortical cells and reticular neurons. <sentence_start/>The novelty was to introduce, in the thalamic compartment, the biophysical effects of direct stimulation. <sentence_start/>Regarding clinical data, we used a quite unique data set recorded in a patient (drug-resistant epilepsy) with a focal cortical dysplasia (FCD). <sentence_start/>In this patient, DBS strongly reduced the sustained epileptic activity of the FCD for low-frequency (LFS, < 2 Hz) and high-frequency stimulation (HFS, > 70 Hz) while intermediate-frequency stimulation (IFS, around 50 Hz) had no effect. <sentence_start/>Signal processing, clustering, and optimization techniques allowed us to identify the necessary conditions for reproducing, in the model, the observed frequency-dependent stimulation effects. <sentence_start/>Key elements which explain the suppression of epileptic activity in the FCD include: (a) feed-forward inhibition and synaptic short-term depression of thalamocortical connections at LFS, and (b) inhibition of the thalamic output at HFS. <sentence_start/>Conversely, modeling results indicate that IFS favors thalamic oscillations and entrains epileptic dynamics.

Deep brain stimulation (DBS) for Parkinson's disease (PD) and other movement and psychiatric disorders-including dystonia, tremor, and depression-is clinically used today as a conventional therapeutic procedure for the alleviation of symptoms (Sillay and Starr, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B65" count="1">2009</citation>). <sentence_start/>Since the early 90s, neurologists also attempted to apply DBS to other neurological disorders, typically to intractable epilepsies in order to suppress-or at least dramatically reduce-the occurrence of seizures [see recent review in Boon et al. (<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B6" doi="10.1016/j.nurt.2008.12.003" pmid="19332313" pmcid="PMC5084197" count="1">2009</citation>)]. <sentence_start/>These studies followed early scientific evidence showing potentially beneficial effects of DBS on epileptic neural dynamics in animal models (Reimer et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B57" doi="10.1016/0013-4694(67)90188-5" pmid="4168976" count="1">1967</citation>; Hablitz, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B26" doi="10.1016/0014-4886(76)90022-4" pmid="1248564" count="1">1976</citation>) as well as in patients (Cooper et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B12" pmid="4206369" count="1">1973</citation>; Davis et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B15" pmid="6977325" doi="10.1159/000101577" count="1">1982</citation>; Wright and Weller, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B84" doi="10.1136/jnnp.46.3.266" pmid="6405013" pmcid="PMC1027335" count="1">1983</citation>). <sentence_start/>However, contrary to PD, the optimal “antiepileptic parameters” of DBS for reducing the frequency of seizures are much more variable among patients and the number of non-responders to stimulation still perplexes scientists. <sentence_start/>Moreover, in responding patients, the fine tuning of stimulation parameters in a patient-specific manner remains indispensable for maximizing antiepileptic effects. <sentence_start/>On that account, many fundamental questions are frequently raised: where and when to stimulate, at which frequency, at which current intensity, and with which current waveform?

The answers to these questions remain bound to our current, and still limited, understanding of the mechanisms by which DBS modulates neuronal dynamics, whether normal or pathological. <sentence_start/>Today, the precise mechanisms of neuronal modulation by DBS remain elusive. <sentence_start/>In addition, these mechanisms are controversial as observed effects are sometimes opposite (McIntyre et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B47" pmid="15134690" doi="10.1016/j.clinph.2003.12.024" count="1">2004b</citation>). <sentence_start/>Among the many studies reported over the last decade, identified mechanisms regarding HFS include: local depolarization blockade by HFS (Beurrier et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B3" pmid="11287459" doi="10.1152/jn.2001.85.4.1351" count="1">2001</citation>), synaptic depression due to neurotransmitter depletion (Shen et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B63" doi="10.1002/syn.10274" pmid="14556236" count="1">2003</citation>; Kim et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B33" doi="10.1152/jn.00276.2011" pmid="22773781" pmcid="PMC3544996" count="1">2012</citation>), synaptic inhibition (Filali et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B19" doi="10.1007/s00221-003-1784-y" pmid="14745464" count="1">2004</citation>), disruption of the thalamocortical network's dysrhythmia (McIntyre and Hahn, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B46" doi="10.1016/j.nbd.2009.09.022" pmid="19804831" pmcid="PMC2862840" count="1">2010</citation>; Kendall et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B32" doi="10.1088/1741-2560/8/4/046001" pmid="21623007" pmcid="PMC3155385" count="1">2011</citation>). <sentence_start/>As far as LFS is concerned, some studies described a transient synaptic depression that alters synaptic transmission (Jiang et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B31" pmid="12736347" doi="10.1523/JNEUROSCI.23-09-03761.2003" pmcid="PMC6742196" count="1">2003</citation>; Speechley et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B67" doi="10.1111/j.1460-9568.2007.05857.x" pmid="17970743" count="1">2007</citation>). <sentence_start/>Finally, IFS is routinely used in the context of presurgical evaluation of patients with drug resistant epilepsy to map epileptogenic and functional brain areas. <sentence_start/>It has long been observed that this type of stimulation is prone to trigger epileptic afterdischarges (Goddard, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B25" doi="10.1038/2141020a0" pmid="6055396" count="1">1967</citation>). <sentence_start/>This brief overview shows that the spectrum of involved mechanisms is very large and that distinct stimulation frequencies trigger distinct cellular/network processes. <sentence_start/>More precise insights into these processes will come with increased knowledge about both biophysical and neurophysiological effects of stimulation currents on underlying neuronal systems.

However, the access to cellular and network mechanisms induced by DBS is rather difficult in animal models of epilepsy and (almost) impossible in patients especially in large-scale systems like the thalamocortical loop. <sentence_start/>An alternative approach is the use of computational models based on physiological data to first reproduce and then explain changes in cerebral activity as a function of stimulation conditions (stimulation site, intensity, and frequency). <sentence_start/>This is precisely the objective of this study, with a special focus on the distinct effects of DBS frequency on cortical epileptic dynamics.

Our investigation combines computational modeling and clinical data. <sentence_start/>We explored stimulation effects in a lumped-parameter mesoscopic neural mass model of the thalamacortical loop, inspired from previously published models (Suffczynski et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B70" doi="10.1016/j.neuroscience.2004.03.014" pmid="15207365" count="1">2004</citation>; Lopes Da Silva, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B37" doi="10.1016/S0079-6123(06)59001-6" pmid="17071220" count="1">2006</citation>; Roberts and Robinson, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B58" doi="10.1016/j.jtbi.2008.03.005" pmid="18407293" count="1">2008</citation>; Crunelli et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B13" pmid="21889315" doi="10.1016/j.eplepsyres.2011.07.011" pmcid="PMC3227737" count="1">2011</citation>).

Although these models are lumped representations of underlying neuronal systems, they offer a number of advantages in the context of this study. <sentence_start/>First, neural mass models include subpopulations of principal excitatory cells and inhibitory interneurons. <sentence_start/>Second, these models were shown to produce realistic activity as observed in LFPs or EEG under normal (Freeman, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B21" count="1">1973</citation>; Lopes Da Silva et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B38" doi="10.1007/BF00270757" pmid="4853232" count="1">1974</citation>) or epileptic conditions [review in Lytton (<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B40" doi="10.1038/nrn2416" pmid="18594562" pmcid="PMC2739976" count="1">2008</citation>); Wendling (<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B79" doi="10.1586/14737175.8.6.889" pmid="18505354" pmcid="PMC2721954" count="1">2008</citation>)]. <sentence_start/>Third, main parameters (mean membrane potential and firing rate) provide access to the investigation of several stimulation-induced (patho)physiological mechanisms. <sentence_start/>For instance, a neural mass model was successfully used in the context of direct low-intensity pulse stimulation in the hippocampus to explain the behavior of evoked responses during the transition to seizures (Suffczynski et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B69" doi="10.1103/PhysRevE.78.051917" pmid="19113165" count="1">2008</citation>).

In particular, using this model, we analyzed the neurophysiological effects induced by direct thalamic stimulation on epileptic cortical dynamics at low frequency (LF, < 20 Hz), intermediate frequency (IF, 20-70 Hz) and high frequency (HF, 70-130 Hz). <sentence_start/>Model parameters were tuned to reproduce a typical pathological oscillatory activity observed in a neocortical lesion (focal cortical dysplasia, or FCD) in a patient with drug-resistant epilepsy. <sentence_start/>Intracerebral EEG (iEEG) signals observed during thalamic stimulation (centromedian nucleus) of this patient revealed particularly pronounced frequency-dependent modulation of the FCD pathological activity. <sentence_start/>Therefore, this data set offered the unique opportunity to identify key model parameters for which such a frequency-dependent modulation could be reproduced and, subsequently to get insights regarding the mechanisms underlying the modulatory effects, in the FCD, of thalamic stimulation. <sentence_start/>Results revealed that LFS favors feed-forward inhibition and short-term depression at the cortical level and that HFS inhibits the thalamic activity, while IFS reinforces reticulothalamic oscillations thus entraining cortical pathological epileptic dynamics.

In this section, we present (1) the neurophysiologically-relevant computational model that we developed to study thalamic DBS, (2) the real depth-EEG dataset used for model tuning and, (3) the signal processing methods used for characterizing real and simulated EEG signals.

In order to study the effects of thalamic DBS on cortical dynamics, we implemented a physiologically-plausible mesoscopic model of the thalamocortical loop. <sentence_start/>This model accounts for the average activity of both cortical and thalamic compartments which include various types of neuronal populations interacting via synaptic transmission. <sentence_start/>This modeling approach was first proposed in the early 70s (Wilson and Cowan, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B83" doi="10.1016/S0006-3495(72)86068-5" pmid="4332108" pmcid="PMC1484078" count="1">1972</citation>) and further enriched in order to interpret electrophysiological recordings and study brain dynamics, in the olfactory (Freeman, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B21" count="1">1973</citation>) and the thalamocortical (Lopes Da Silva et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B38" doi="10.1007/BF00270757" pmid="4853232" count="1">1974</citation>) system, for instance, as well as the dynamics of cortical oscillations (Nunez, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B51" doi="10.1016/0025-5564(74)90020-0" count="1">1974</citation>). <sentence_start/>This approach was then developed by other research groups in the context of state changes in brain dynamics (Wright et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B85" doi="10.1007/BF00355686" pmid="4074768" count="1">1985</citation>), visual evoked potentials (Jansen et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B29" doi="10.1007/BF00224863" pmid="8452897" count="1">1993</citation>), dynamics of the human alpha rhythm (Stam et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B68" pmid="10574295" doi="10.1016/s1388-2457(99)00099-1" count="1">1999</citation>) or pathophysiological mechanisms of ictal transitions in epilepsy (Wendling et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B82" doi="10.1007/s004220000160" pmid="11039701" count="1">2000</citation>, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B80" doi="10.1046/j.1460-9568.2002.01985.x" pmid="12028360" count="1">2002</citation>; Suffczynski et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B71" doi="10.1016/S0167-8760(01)00177-5" pmid="11742683" count="1">2001</citation>; Robinson et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B59" doi="10.1103/PhysRevE.65.041924" pmid="12005890" count="1">2002</citation>; Liley and Bojak, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B35" pmid="16357635" count="1">2005</citation>; Breakspear et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B9" doi="10.1093/cercor/bhj072" pmid="16280462" count="1">2006</citation>). <sentence_start/>Later, neural mass models were also used in studies dealing with the connectivity among cortical regions and the impact of model parameters on the power spectrum of EEG or MEG signals (Robinson et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B60" doi="10.1103/PhysRevE.56.826" count="1">1997</citation>; David and Friston, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B14" doi="10.1016/j.neuroimage.2003.07.015" pmid="14642484" count="1">2003</citation>; Zavaglia et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B86" doi="10.1016/j.jneumeth.2006.04.022" pmid="16757033" count="1">2006</citation>).

The model architecture was inspired from previously published models of the thalamocortical loop (Suffczynski et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B70" doi="10.1016/j.neuroscience.2004.03.014" pmid="15207365" count="1">2004</citation>; Lopes Da Silva, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B37" doi="10.1016/S0079-6123(06)59001-6" pmid="17071220" count="1">2006</citation>; Roberts and Robinson, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B58" doi="10.1016/j.jtbi.2008.03.005" pmid="18407293" count="1">2008</citation>; Crunelli et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B13" pmid="21889315" doi="10.1016/j.eplepsyres.2011.07.011" pmcid="PMC3227737" count="1">2011</citation>). <sentence_start/>In a global view, the model was built of three interconnected compartments: a cortical compartment, a thalamic compartment, and a reticular compartment, in accordance with previously published models (Figure 1A) and with anatomical data (Figure 1B). <sentence_start/>Each compartment includes one or several subpopulation(s) of neurons, either excitatory or inhibitory. <sentence_start/>Generally speaking, the input/output functions of a considered subpopulation are represented by two mathematical equations that were respectively named “pulse-to-wave” (input) and “wave-to-pulse” (output) by Walter Freeman (Freeman, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B22" doi="10.1142/S0218127492000653" count="1">1992</citation>). <sentence_start/>The former is a linear transfer function that converts the presynaptic average density of afferent action potentials into an average postsynaptic membrane potential (PSP), either excitatory (EPSP) or inhibitory (IPSP). <sentence_start/>The output function is a static nonlinear function (sigmoid) that provides the average pulse density of action potentials fired by neurons depending on the sum of EPSPs and IPSPs at the input. <sentence_start/>This non-linear function accounts for threshold and saturation effects that take place at the somas and initial axonal segments of considered cells.

(A)</bold> The model architecture comprises three main compartments: cortical, thalamic, and reticular. <sentence_start/>The cortical compartment includes three subpopulations: P (pyramidal principal neurons), <italic toggle="yes">I<sup>C</sup></italic><sub>1</sub> (soma- and proximal-dendrite targeting interneurons mediating GABA<italic toggle="yes"><sub>A, fast</sub></italic> currents), and <italic toggle="yes">I<sup>C</sup></italic><sub>2</sub>, (dendrite-targeting interneurons mediating GABA<italic toggle="yes"><sub>A, slow</sub></italic> currents). <sentence_start/>The thalamic compartment represents a generic thalamic nucleus including a subpopulation of excitatory thalamocortical (<italic toggle="yes">TC</italic>) cells. <sentence_start/>The reticular nucleus (RtN) compartment is made up of two GABAergic neuronal populations (<italic toggle="yes">I</italic><italic toggle="yes"><sup>Rt</sup></italic><sub>1</sub>, GABA<italic toggle="yes"><sub>A, fast</sub></italic> currents and <italic toggle="yes">I<sup>Rt</sup></italic><sub>2</sub>, GABA<italic toggle="yes"><sub>A, slow</sub></italic>). <sentence_start/>Excitatory synaptic transmission among the considered subpopulations is glutamatergic (GLU). <sentence_start/><bold>(B)</bold> <italic toggle="yes">Anatomical connectivity of the CMN, PMC, and RtN</italic>. <sentence_start/>This diagram represents the anatomy of a particular thalamocortical loop interconnecting the CM thalamic nucleus, the PMC, and the RtN. <sentence_start/>Connectivity patterns were inferred from the literature. <sentence_start/>It is compatible with the thalamocortical model diagram presented in <bold>(A)</bold>.

The cortical compartment was inspired from an existing model of the neocortex which proved its capability of generating both normal and epileptiform activity. <sentence_start/>Readers may refer to Molaee-Ardekani et al. (<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B49" doi="10.1016/j.neuroimage.2009.12.049" pmid="20034581" count="1">2010</citation>) for details. <sentence_start/>In brief, the cortical compartment integrates a subpopulation of pyramidal cells (<italic toggle="yes">P</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">W</italic> = <italic toggle="yes">A</italic><italic toggle="yes"><sub>C</sub></italic>, τ<italic toggle="yes"><sub>w</sub></italic> = τ<italic toggle="yes"><sub>ac</sub></italic> in Equation 1) and two inhibitory neuronal populations (<italic toggle="yes">I<sup>c</sup></italic><sub>1</sub> and <italic toggle="yes">I<sup>c</sup></italic><sub>2</sub>, Figure 1A) representing soma- and proximal-dendrite targeting interneurons (GABA<italic toggle="yes"><sub>A, fast</sub></italic> currents, <italic toggle="yes">W</italic> = <italic toggle="yes">G<sub>C</sub></italic>, τ<italic toggle="yes"><sub>w</sub></italic> = τ<italic toggle="yes"><sub>gc</sub></italic> in Equation 1) and dendrite-targeting interneurons (GABA<italic toggle="yes"><sub>A, slow</sub></italic> currents, <italic toggle="yes">W</italic> = <italic toggle="yes">B<sub>C</sub></italic>, τ<italic toggle="yes"><sub>w</sub></italic> = τ<italic toggle="yes"><sub>bc</sub></italic> in Equation 1), respectively. <sentence_start/>Pyramidal collateral excitation was implemented as in Jansen et al. (<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B29" doi="10.1007/BF00224863" pmid="8452897" count="1">1993</citation>).

In addition, these three cortical subpopulations receive excitatory input from the thalamic compartment. <sentence_start/>Therefore, feed-forward inhibition (FFI) is represented in the model as the two subpopulations of interneurons project to the pyramidal subpopulation (see <italic toggle="yes">The Thalamic and Reticular Compartments</italic> paragraph below).

STD is present in the neocortex (Boudreau and Ferster, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B7" doi="10.1523/JNEUROSCI.1445-05.2005" pmid="16079400" pmcid="PMC6725224" count="1">2005</citation>). <sentence_start/>It can be potentially involved in the context of direct stimulation of the thalamus as TC cells directly project to cortical pyramidal cells. <sentence_start/>Consequently, this mechanism was implemented at the interface of thalamic/cortical compartments. <sentence_start/>To our knowledge, an implementation of STD in neural mass models has not been proposed before.

In our model, we represented a modulatory effect of the amplitude of the average EPSP (parameter <italic toggle="yes">A<sub>C</sub></italic>') at the level of subpopulation <italic toggle="yes">P</italic> depending on the density of action potentials [<italic toggle="yes">d<sub>AP</sub></italic>(<italic toggle="yes">t</italic>)] coming from the thalamic compartment. <sentence_start/>This modulatory effect was obtained by multiplying <italic toggle="yes">A<sub>C</sub></italic>' by a time-varying coefficient κ(<italic toggle="yes">t</italic>) ∈ [0.6, 1] where the function describing the evolution of κ(<italic toggle="yes">t</italic>) was derived from Chung et al. (<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B11" doi="10.1016/S0896-6273(02)00659-1" pmid="11988174" count="1">2002</citation>). <sentence_start/>This study shows that: (i) cortical EPSPs drop by 40% under periodic low-frequency intense thalamocortical (<italic toggle="yes">TC</italic>) cell firing and, (ii) this drop in cortical EPSP is directly linked to transient depression of thalamocortical monosynaptic projections to pyramidal neurons.

In line with these observations, STD was implemented as follows. <sentence_start/>First, signal <italic toggle="yes">d</italic><sup>(<italic toggle="yes">t</italic>)</sup><italic toggle="yes"><sub>AP</sub></italic> is low-pass filtered (cutoff frequency = 10 Hz) to restrict the STD effect to LFS. <sentence_start/>Then, from each time <italic toggle="yes">t</italic><sub>η</sub> at which the filtered signal <italic toggle="yes">d<sup>f</sup><sub>AP</sub></italic>(<italic toggle="yes">t</italic>) exceeds a firing rate equal to η, the κ(<italic toggle="yes">t</italic>) coefficient undertakes an exponential decay given by κ (<italic toggle="yes">t</italic>) = κ<sub>η</sub> · <italic toggle="yes">e</italic><sup>−<italic toggle="yes">t</italic>/τ</sup> where κ<sub>η</sub> = κ(<italic toggle="yes">t</italic><sup>−</sup><sub>η</sub>) and where <italic toggle="yes">t</italic><sup>−</sup><sub>η</sub> is the time instant that just precedes <italic toggle="yes">t</italic><sub>η</sub>. <sentence_start/>The decrease of κ(<italic toggle="yes">t</italic>) is limited to the time interval [<italic toggle="yes">t</italic><sub>η</sub> + 0.45 s] and cannot exceed 40%, total. <sentence_start/>Parameters η and τ were set to 0.8 and 8 s, respectively.

interneurons. <sentence_start/>The activation of these GABAergic interneurons subsequently promotes inhibition of pyramidal cells after a di-synaptic delay. <sentence_start/>Therefore, <italic toggle="yes">TC</italic> cells activation induces first an EPSP followed later on by an IPSP on cortical pyramidal cells, resulting in feed-forward inhibition (FFI). <sentence_start/>The <italic state) relatively to the amount of time they do not fire (down state). <sentence_start/>Figure 8B provides the evolution of the <italic toggle="yes">HtoLR</italic> when the stimulation frequency is progressively changing from 0 to 150 Hz in the model. <sentence_start/>As depicted, these simulations indicated that three stimulation frequency ranges have dramatic effects on the firing of <italic toggle="yes">TC</italic> cells. <sentence_start/>First, from 0 to 20 Hz, the down state is predominant. <sentence_start/>Then, an abrupt jump was observed around 22 Hz indicating that beyond this value, the firing rate dramatically increased. <sentence_start/>Interestingly, from 55 to 65 Hz, a progressive decrease of the <italic toggle="yes">HtoLR</italic> was observed. <sentence_start/>Then, after 70 Hz, the ratio is equal to zero indicating that <italic toggle="yes">TC</italic> cells did not fire anymore. <sentence_start/>Finally, in order to relate the thalamic activity with the cortical activity, we plotted the phase portraits (<italic toggle="yes">TC</italic> cell firing vs. cortical LFP) as illustrated in Figure 8C. Results confirmed the visual inspection of signals simulated at the two sites. <sentence_start/>For the no stimulation (NS) and for the intermediate frequency stimulation (IFS) conditions, phase portraits were found to be quite similar. <sentence_start/>They indicated the presence of mixed slow/fast oscillations in both signals. <sentence_start/>For the low frequency stimulation (LFS) condition, oscillations in the simulated LFP in the FCD were reduced. <sentence_start/>They came along with short-duration, abrupt and rhythmic augmentations of the <italic toggle="yes">TC</italic> firing corresponding to stimulation pulses. <sentence_start/>Finally, for the high frequency stimulation (HFS) condition, oscillations in both types of activity stayed confined to small amplitude values.

We modeled the thalamocortical loop in order to investigate frequency-dependent effects of electrical stimulation performed in the thalamus and aimed at modulating the neocortical activity. <sentence_start/>We chose to elaborate our model at a mesoscopic level, i.e., intermediate between microsocopic and macroscopic.

Regarding the model architecture, we followed a similar approach to that used in previously proposed models of the thalamocortical loop (Robinson et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B59" doi="10.1103/PhysRevE.65.041924" pmid="12005890" count="1">2002</citation>; Suffczynski et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B70" doi="10.1016/j.neuroscience.2004.03.014" pmid="15207365" count="1">2004</citation>; Breakspear et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B9" doi="10.1093/cercor/bhj072" pmid="16280462" count="1">2006</citation>; Roberts and Robinson, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B58" doi="10.1016/j.jtbi.2008.03.005" pmid="18407293" count="1">2008</citation>; Marten et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B44" doi="10.1098/rsta.2008.0255" pmid="19218156" count="1">2009</citation>; Crunelli et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B13" pmid="21889315" doi="10.1016/j.eplepsyres.2011.07.011" pmcid="PMC3227737" count="1">2011</citation>). <sentence_start/>Our model includes three main compartments: cerebral cortex, reticular nucleus and thalamic relay. <sentence_start/>Subpopulations of neurons and interneurons located in these three structures interact via excitatory and/or inhibitory synaptic connections. <sentence_start/>The novelty with respect to aforementioned studies is threefold. <sentence_start/>First, we modified the cortical compartment in order to better approximate the temporal dynamics of epileptic signals recorded in the FCD. <sentence_start/>This modification consisted in the use of two types of interneurons (mediating GABAergic IPSPs with slow and fast kinetics on cortical principal cells), as reported in a previous study (Molaee-Ardekani et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B49" doi="10.1016/j.neuroimage.2009.12.049" pmid="20034581" count="1">2010</citation>). <sentence_start/>Second, our model accounts for the direct effects of electrical stimulation. <sentence_start/>At this stage, we used the assumption according to which the perturbation of the mean membrane potential of neurons is a linear function of the electrical field magnitude induced by bipolar stimulation. <sentence_start/>This “λE” assumption was already used in neural mass models in the context of low-intensity direct hippocampal stimulation to anticipate seizures (Suffczynski et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B69" doi="10.1103/PhysRevE.78.051917" pmid="19113165" count="1">2008</citation>) as well as in the analysis of the stimulus-response relationship of DBS in healthy animals (Adhikari et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B1" doi="10.1016/j.jneumeth.2009.06.044" pmid="19616579" count="1">2009</citation>). <sentence_start/>However, it is worth mentioning that in our model, the three subtypes of neurons (<italic toggle="yes">TC</italic> cells and both subpopulations of inhibitory neurons in the RtN) are depolarized by the stimulation, as suggested in (Molaee-Ardekani et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B50" doi="10.1016/j.brs.2011.12.006" pmid="22420944" count="1">2013</citation>) and conversely to (Adhikari et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B1" doi="10.1016/j.jneumeth.2009.06.044" pmid="19616579" count="1">2009</citation>) where only principal cells are impacted. <sentence_start/>And third, our model includes two well-known mechanisms at the cortical level: feed-forward inhibition (FFI) and short-term depression (STD).

As in any modeling approach, our approach has some limitations. <sentence_start/>First, the chosen modeling level does not allow for analyzing sub-cellular mechanisms involved in stimulation-evoked changes. <sentence_start/>Similarly, it does not account for direct activation of axons by stimulation vs. somatic inhibition (McIntyre et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B47" pmid="15134690" doi="10.1016/j.clinph.2003.12.024" count="1">2004b</citation>), nor for the mechanisms of orthodromic/antidromic propagation of action potentials due to stimulation (Degos et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B16" doi="10.1523/JNEUROSCI.1056-05.2005" pmid="16107655" pmcid="PMC6725399" count="1">2005</citation>; Hammond et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B27" doi="10.1016/j.tins.2007.05.004" pmid="17532060" count="1">2007</citation>; Dorval et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B17" doi="10.1152/jn.90763.2008" pmid="18784271" pmcid="PMC2585386" count="1">2008</citation>). <sentence_start/>Second, a strong assumption in the type of model we used (neural mass) is related to the intrinsic synchronization among neurons included in a given sub-population. <sentence_start/>This assumption does not allow for representing either de- or weakly-synchronized firing patterns that may be observed during epileptic activity, in particular during high frequency oscillations that can be encountered in FCDs (Brázdil et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B8" doi="10.1016/j.eplepsyres.2010.03.003" pmid="20362416" count="1">2010</citation>). <sentence_start/>Nevertheless, we could accurately reproduce the abnormal rhythms generated in the FCD suggesting that main pyramidal cells have a relatively synchronized activity in this epileptogenic tissue. <sentence_start/>Third, regarding plasticity-related mechanisms, we only implemented short-term effects (i.e., STD) and neglected long-term plastic changes that may be induced by DBS (Shukla et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B64" doi="10.1136/jnnp-2012-304102" pmid="23616568" count="1">2013</citation>).

Despite these limitations, we could identify a number of mesoscopic factors which could explain the frequency-dependent mechanisms of thalamic stimulation. <sentence_start/>The model was tuned using electrophysiological data recorded in a patient in whom the centromedian nucleus (CMN) stimulation was particularly efficient to reduce the epileptic activity of a FCD located in the premotor cortex, in a frequency-specific manner. <sentence_start/>The main findings are summarized in Figure 9.

<bold>Frequency-dependent mechanisms underlying DBS. (A)</bold> Under the no stimulation (NS) condition, the thalamocortical loop is responsible for pathological oscillatory rhythms observed in the FCD. <sentence_start/><bold>(B)</bold> For low-frequency stimulation (LFS), feed-forward inhibition (FFI, i.e., excitation of inhibitory cortical interneurons by <italic toggle="yes">TC</italic> cells) and short-term depression (STD, i.e., decreased excitatory synaptic efficacy in thalamus-to-cortex connections) was found to play a major role for the abortion of epileptic activity in the FCD. <sentence_start/><bold>(C)</bold> For the intermediate-frequency stimulation (IFS) condition, thalamic output is reinforced (increase of <italic toggle="yes">TC</italic> cells firing) leading to an increase of the average excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP) on cortical pyramidal cells and to no “anti-epileptic” effect. <sentence_start/><bold>(D)</bold> For high-frequency stimulation (HFS), the direct and sustained excitation of reticular nucleus (RtN) interneurons leads to dramatic decrease of <italic toggle="yes">TC</italic> cells firing rate and to a suppression of epileptic activity.

In the model, under the NS condition, excitation among pyramidal cells had to be increased and inhibition had to be reduced in the cortical compartment for producing “pathological” oscillatory rhythms, as observed in the FCD. <sentence_start/>The thalamocortical loop was found to be responsible for these pathological dynamics, characteristic of FCDs. <sentence_start/>These findings are in line with histological studies showing that these typical oscillations are generated in altered brain tissue, where inhibition is partially deteriorated or dysfunctioning (Calcagnotto et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B10" doi="10.1523/JNEUROSCI.2687-05.2005" pmid="16237169" pmcid="PMC6725719" count="1">2005</citation>), and where excitation is heavily increased (Avoli et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B2" pmid="14617420" count="1">2003</citation>). <sentence_start/>In addition to neuron alterations in the dysplastic tissue (Sisodiya et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B66" doi="10.1016/S1474-4422(09)70201-7" pmid="19679275" count="1">2009</citation>), FCD keeps sufficient projections to-and input from-other brain structures to propagate pathological dynamics (Avoli et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B2" pmid="14617420" count="1">2003</citation>). <sentence_start/>As mentioned, the presence of connections with subcortical structures was a necessary condition in the model for producing pathological oscillations resembling those actually recorded in the FCD (Figure 9A).

For the low-frequency stimulation (LFS, <italic toggle="yes">f</italic> < 20 Hz) condition, two mechanisms were found to play a major role for the abortion of epileptic activity in the FCD: short-term depression (STD, i.e., decreased excitatory synaptic efficacy in thalamus-to-cortex connections) and feed-forward inhibition (FFI, i.e., excitation of inhibitory cortical interneurons by <italic toggle="yes">TC</italic> cells) (Figure 9B).

STD was reported in previous studies concerning cortical adaptation to thalamic stimulation, and suggesting that electrical LFS of <italic toggle="yes">TC</italic> cell axons <italic toggle="yes">in vivo</italic> resulted in a 40% reduction in cortical EPSPs (Chung et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B11" doi="10.1016/S0896-6273(02)00659-1" pmid="11988174" count="1">2002</citation>). <sentence_start/>In the same context, LFS trains in adult anaesthetized rats provoked transient long-term depression of thalamocortical synapses; this was measured by up to 40% drop in cortical EPSPs after LFS trains and under the effect of GABA antagonist (Speechley et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B67" doi="10.1111/j.1460-9568.2007.05857.x" pmid="17970743" count="1">2007</citation>).

As mentioned above, the LFS effects could not be reproduced by the model without incorporating also FFI. <sentence_start/>Actually, thalamocortical ascending fibers directly target pyramidal neurons as well as cortical GABAergic interneurons inducing EPSPs in both cell types (Pouille and Scanziani, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B54" doi="10.1126/science.1060342" pmid="11498596" count="1">2001</citation>). <sentence_start/>In the model, while less efficient (STD) thalamic EPSPs arrive directly onto pyramidal neurons, IPSPs induced by thalamic stimulation also arrive on pyramidal neurons (FFI) lagging by 1-2 ms. <sentence_start/>This short latency between the onset of thalamocortical excitation and the onset of feed-forward inhibition presents a temporal “window of opportunity” for pyramidal cells to integrate excitatory and inhibitory inputs, thus keeping the transmembrane potential below firing threshold. <sentence_start/>In the literature, neuroanatomical and neurophysiological studies (Isaacson and Scanziani, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B28" doi="10.1016/j.neuron.2011.09.027" pmid="22017986" pmcid="PMC3236361" count="1">2011</citation>) showed the functional importance of FFI in regulating cortical dynamics by controlling cortical excitability (Gabernet et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B24" doi="10.1016/j.neuron.2005.09.022" pmid="16242411" count="1">2005</citation>). <sentence_start/>Our study suggests that LFS regulates cortical excitability by a dual mechanism of FFI and STD (Figure 9B).

For the intermediate-frequency stimulation (IFS, 20 < <italic toggle="yes">f</italic> < 70 Hz) condition, results indicated that the thalamic output is reinforced (increase of <italic toggle="yes">TC</italic> cells firing) and leads to an increase of the average excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP) on cortical pyramidal cells (Figure 9C). <sentence_start/>This effect corresponds to an increase of the spatiotemporal summation of unitary EPSPs. <sentence_start/>In this case, both the cortical excitability and the gain in the excitatory thalamocortical loop is increased, leading to “no anti-epileptic” effect. <sentence_start/>We did not find much studies using DBS stimulation in the intermediate frequency range of (20-60 Hz) in the context of epilepsy. <sentence_start/>Nevertheless, it is noteworthy that 50 Hz stimulation frequency is classically used during the presurgical evaluation of patient with intractable partial epilepsy in order to trigger seizures and delineate the epileptogenic zone (Talairach et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B72" pmid="4603712" count="1">1974</citation>; Jayakar et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B30" doi="10.1097/00004691-199204010-00009" pmid="1592899" count="1">1992</citation>). <sentence_start/>The same frequency range is also known to provoke afterdischarges and was actually used in the kindling model of epilepsy (Goddard, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B25" doi="10.1038/2141020a0" pmid="6055396" count="1">1967</citation>; Racine, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B55" doi="10.1016/0013-4694(72)90177-0" pmid="4110397" count="1">1972</citation>).

Finally, for the high-frequency stimulation (HFS, <italic toggle="yes">f</italic> > 70 Hz) condition, the direct and sustained excitation of reticular nucleus (RtN) interneurons leads to strong inhibition of <italic toggle="yes">TC</italic> cells and thus to dramatic decrease of their firing rate. <sentence_start/>Despite the fact that <italic toggle="yes">TC</italic> neurons are also affected by stimulation, the response of reticular GABAergic neurons to stimulation and the higher efficiency of GABA-mediated currents ensure that IPSPs override EPSPs on <italic toggle="yes">TC</italic> cells. <sentence_start/>In this case, the reduced excitatory input to cortical pyramidal cells also leads to a suppression of epileptic activity (Figure 9D). <sentence_start/>This result corroborates reported stimulation studies where HFS (>100 Hz) was associated with significant decrease in epileptiform discharges <italic toggle="yes">in vitro</italic>, and reduction in seizure frequency in responding patients (Velasco et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B73" doi="10.1111/j.1528-1167.2006.00593.x" pmid="16886984" count="1">2006</citation>; Fisher et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B20" doi="10.1111/j.1528-1167.2010.02536.x" pmid="20331461" count="1">2010</citation>). <sentence_start/>This hypothesis is in line with recent findings suggesting that HFS of the globus pallidus (GPi) in dystonia patients decreased its firing by stimulation-evoked GABA release from afferent fibers and thereby the enhancement of inhibitory synaptic transmission by HFS (Liu et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B36" doi="10.1152/jn.00527.2011" pmid="22457462" count="1">2012</citation>). <sentence_start/>Similarly, HFS (100-130 Hz) of the STN neurons in vitro showed a suppression of the activity of the majority of neurons by the reinforcement of inhibitory responses (Filali et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B19" doi="10.1007/s00221-003-1784-y" pmid="14745464" count="1">2004</citation>). <sentence_start/>Other HFS studies also provided evidence on the inhibition of GPi output during HFS in human patients (Dostrovsky et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B18" pmid="10899228" doi="10.1152/jn.2000.84.1.570" count="1">2000</citation>) as well as the disruption thalamocortical network's dysrhythmia (McIntyre and Hahn, <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B46" doi="10.1016/j.nbd.2009.09.022" pmid="19804831" pmcid="PMC2862840" count="1">2010</citation>; Kendall et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B32" doi="10.1088/1741-2560/8/4/046001" pmid="21623007" pmcid="PMC3155385" count="1">2011</citation>).

In epilepsy research, it is well-admitted that there is, unfortunately, a lack of tangible results regarding the effects of electrical stimulation in the brain. <sentence_start/>Therefore, the very crucial issue of choosing the “optimal” stimulation parameters remains unsolved, whatever the stimulation procedure. <sentence_start/>Although computational models are always based on a number of simplifying assumptions, we think that they provide an efficient framework to (i) account for the many and essential factors that may intervene during stimulation procedures and (ii) analyze the links between these factors in a formal manner. <sentence_start/>This approach is particularly fruitful when models are well grounded in experimental/clinical data (Wendling et al., <citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B81" doi="10.1111/j.1460-9568.2012.08039.x" pmid="22805062" count="1">2012</citation>). <sentence_start/>This is somehow a weak point of this study since we could make use of data sets recorded in one patient only. <sentence_start/>However, it should be mentioned that these very informative data sets stay relatively rare since many conditions have to be met (patient candidate to surgery, FCD, electrodes positioned in appropriate structures).

At this stage, the face value of the model is satisfactory. <sentence_start/>The next step is obviously to test the model predictions using animal models. <sentence_start/>Experiments can be undertaken in rodents with electrodes implanted in the cerebral cortex and in the thalamus. <sentence_start/>First, we could start with control animals to assess the modulation of cortical rhythms during/after direct thalamic stimulation at various frequencies and for controlled vigilance states (sleep, awake, resting, exploratory). <sentence_start/>In these controls, some drugs can be used to alter some parameters related to synaptic transmission (in a more or less specific manner) which have a correspondence in the model, on the other hand. <sentence_start/>Then, refined experimental models could be introduced to get closer to the epilepsy context including models of developmental dysplastic lesions [see review in Schwartzkroin and Wenzel (<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B62" doi="10.1111/j.1528-1167.2012.03473.x" pmid="22612807" count="1">2012</citation>)]. <sentence_start/>Hopefully, this combined computational/experimental approach will help us to disclose some of the highly intricate effects of DBS either at local or at network level.
